etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French militant, from Latin mīlitāns, present participle of mīlitāre (“to serve as a soldier”).

definitions.definition: Fighting or disposed to fight; belligerent, warlike. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 2012, Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers, Penguin, published 2013, page 394:
quote.text: The upper tiers of the foreign ministry were quick to embrace a militant policy.

definitions.definition: Aggressively supporting of a political or social cause; adamant, combative. [from 17th c.]
An entrenched or aggressive adherent to a particular cause, now especially a member of a particular ideological faction. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 1976 December 11, Thom Willenbecher, quoting Jean O'Leary, “Women's Caucus Quits Gay Academic Union”, in Gay Community News, volume 4, number 24, page 1:
quote.text: [Jim Owles] lamented the declining influence of militant organizations and tactics, stating that militants "help keep the rest of us honest," and prevent moderates from selling out.

quote.citation: 2008, Militants in Pakistan release 250 schoolchildren after taking them hostage, Wikinews:
quote.text: Officials in Pakistan have confirmed that at least 250 schoolchildren between 12 and 18 years old and several teachers were taken hostage by at least seven militants inside a high school in Domail.

definitions.definition: (specifically, communism) someone who supports the Trotskyist political view expressed in the newspaper Militant, or who engages in aggressive left-wing politics. [from 20th c.]
